h1: Honey and toffee notes that creep into pale beer as it ages
title: Honey and Toffee Notes in Old Pale Beer | Craft Beer School
desc: Why a pale lager or pale ale starts to taste of honey, toffee and cardboard as it ages and how to tell staling from diacetyl or crystal malt.
teaser: A pale lager that tastes of honey was not brewed with honey. It was probably stored too long, too warm.
standfirst: Honey and toffee sound like compliments. In a pale lager or pale ale they are usually the first signs of staling, arriving before the cardboard. Here is what is happening in the bottle and how to tell it apart from flavours the brewer put there on purpose.
sections:
Fresh pale beer tastes of bread, crackers and clean malt, with bright hop aroma on top. As it ages, that brightness dulls. A sweet, slightly sticky honey note appears, then a caramel or toffee edge. Hop aroma fades. Bitterness softens. Later, papery and cardboard notes arrive, often with a sweetish, stale finish. Colour can darken slightly too.

Drinkers often describe the honey stage as rounder or sweeter without realising it is a fault. Taste the same beer fresh from the brewery and you notice at once how much it has lost.

Staling is a slow set of chemical reactions driven largely by oxygen and heat. Several groups of compounds change at once:

  • Honey and dried fruit notes come partly from compounds such as beta-damascenone, which tends to rise as beer ages.
  • Caramel and toffee come from slow browning reactions between sugars and amino acids, similar in kind to the reactions in a kiln or a pan, only far slower.
  • Cardboard comes largely from trans-2-nonenal and other aldehydes formed through oxidation of fats and alcohols.
  • Hop aroma breaks down and bitterness falls as iso-alpha acids degrade.

The honey and toffee notes usually show before the cardboard, which is why they are the early warning. Our guide to oxidised beer covers the later stage.

A widely quoted rule of thumb in brewing holds that staling roughly doubles for every 10 °C rise in storage temperature. In practical terms, a pale lager kept at 30 °C for a month can taste older than the same beer kept at 4 °C for several months. Brewers use this effect deliberately in forced ageing tests, holding beer warm for a set time to predict how it will taste later.

In India this matters a great deal. Beer often travels long distances in unrefrigerated trucks, sits in warm warehouses and waits on shop shelves before going into a fridge. A pale beer can pick up honey and toffee notes well before its best before date if the cold chain breaks.

Honey and toffee are not always faults. Three other sources produce similar flavours:

  • Crystal and caramel malts. Amber ales, bitters and many malt-led beers are brewed to taste of toffee and caramel. That character is fresh and clean, not stale.
  • Honey itself. Some beers, such as braggots and honey ales, are brewed with honey.
  • Diacetyl. Butter and butterscotch from fermentation, often with a slick feel on the tongue. It can be mistaken for toffee. Our guide to diacetyl explains how to tell them apart.

The clue is context. A pale lager or a hop-led pale ale should not taste of toffee. If it does and there is no crystal malt or honey in the recipe, staling is the likely cause.
How to check a beer's freshness

Most packaged beer carries a best before date, a packaging date or a batch code. Pale lagers and hoppy beers are at their best well before that date. Rules of thumb:

  • Look for the packaging date where it is printed and buy the freshest stock.
  • Buy from shops that keep beer in a fridge rather than on a warm shelf.
  • Keep pale beer cold at home and drink it within weeks rather than months.
  • Do not age pale beer. It does not improve.

If you want to see staling for yourself, buy two cans of the same pale lager. Put one in the fridge and leave the other in a warm cupboard for a month, then taste them side by side. The honey note in the warm can is usually obvious.
Hoppy beers stale fastest of all

Pale lagers are not the only victims. Hazy IPAs and pale ales lose their fresh hop aroma within weeks at warm temperatures and the honey and toffee notes arrive into the gap. Many brewers of heavily hopped beers print a canning date rather than only a best before date and ask shops to keep them cold for this reason. A hoppy beer that smells more of honey than of citrus has already lost most of what you paid for.

The same reactions that ruin a pale lager can improve a barleywine or imperial stout, where honey, toffee and dried fruit fit the style. Our guide to sherry and raisin notes in aged beer covers that side. The difference lies in the beer's strength, malt richness and lack of delicate hop aroma.

Your first step: next time you buy a pale lager, find the packaging or best before date, taste it carefully and note any honey or toffee. Then compare it with a fresher can from a cold fridge.
faqs: Why does my pale lager taste of honey?
Usually staling. Oxygen and heat create honey, toffee and later cardboard notes as pale beer ages.
Is toffee flavour in beer a fault?
In pale lagers and hop-led pale ales it usually means staling. In amber ales and malty styles made with crystal malt it is intended.
How fast does beer go stale in the heat?
A common rule of thumb is that staling roughly doubles for every 10 °C rise in storage temperature.
How can I tell staling from diacetyl?
Diacetyl tastes of butter or butterscotch with a slick mouthfeel. Staling brings honey and toffee with dulled hops and, later, cardboard.
